A1.justification: Both PDFs describe LENS and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A-G. Added material, renumbered tables, and relocated content can be matched reliably.

before.justification: V1 reports original narrative-generation experiments using 50,957 EMAs from 258 participants, ablation and scaling studies, and a 13-expert evaluation of 117 narratives.

after.justification: V2 retains these empirical results and adds encoder-sensitivity experiments, a sensor-mismatch experiment, and analyses of the collected symptom responses.

M1.justification: The stated text-embedding treatment changes: v1 Figure 4 describes a frozen text embedder, whereas v2 Section 3.2.3 explicitly includes it among updated parameters. The encoder, fusion procedure, objective, and two-stage curriculum otherwise remain unchanged. The PDFs do not establish whether this reflects retraining or a correction to the earlier description.

E1.justification: V2 adds a corrupted-input test scenario with sensor streams shuffled across participants while questions and labels remain fixed. The cohort and clinical tasks remain unchanged. The correction from 13 to 14 EMA items does not establish expanded coverage: v1 Table 2 already lists those items.

E2.justification: TS-Text and TS-Image remain the main comparators, and TS-Text-FT remains the comparator in the encoder ablation. The new encoder configurations and shuffled-input condition are controls for LENS, not added competing methods.

E3.justification: New protocols vary encoder depth over 3, 5, and 7 layers and patch size over 4, 8, and 16 under the 10% training-data setting, and shuffle sensor inputs on the full narrative test set. Existing participant splits, preprocessing, metrics, and expert-study procedures are retained.

E4.justification: Appendix E substantially extends the existing encoder-removal, scaling, efficiency, and qualitative analyses. New experiments directly test dependence on correctly matched sensor inputs and sensitivity to encoder depth and patch size; additional analyses examine construction costs and symptom distributions (Tables 7-10). The sensor-mismatch control addresses a central validity question not directly tested in v1.

E5.justification: Both versions use the same per-rater aggregation, paired t-tests, Bonferroni correction, and Cohen's dz. V2 adds citations for these procedures but introduces no new seed counts, repeated-run reporting, confidence intervals, or statistical uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Existing benchmark, scaling, and expert-study results are retained. Added Table 8 reports Presence Alignment decreasing from 0.601 to 0.480 under sensor mismatch, with ROUGE-L changing from 0.410 to 0.408 and BERTScore from 0.776 to 0.775. Tables 7, 9, and 10 add sensitivity, estimated-cost, and symptom-distribution results. These are targeted new analyses, not same-setting performance improvements.

T1.justification: The normalization, patch construction, multimodal fusion, autoregressive objective, and Appendix D metric definitions are mathematically unchanged. Renaming patch-width and encoder symbols does not introduce new mathematical reasoning, assumptions, or proofs.

C1.justification: The introduction explicitly narrows the intended application to pre-consultation monitoring of people already receiving depression or anxiety care, excluding population screening and diagnosis. The abstract, conclusion, and three principal contributions otherwise retain their scientific scope.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations separating learned language style from sensor-dependent clinical content, discusses encoder robustness and within-cohort symptom variability, and acknowledges untested robustness beyond the Qwen family. It also clarifies that dataset construction is offline. However, its assertion that all sensitivity changes stay within 0.01 contradicts Table 7.

D1.justification: V2 adds a code-availability link and specifies NDA institutional access requirements instead of the vague post-embargo data-release statement. It also discloses SGLang use, API-equivalent construction-cost estimates, and expert recruitment through UpWork and therapist forums with $50-$150 hourly compensation. These disclosures do not establish changes to the retained experiments.

R1.justification: V2 adds citations concerning sensing, statistical methods, heterogeneous-device learning, multimodal reasoning, benchmark quality, and long-tail generation, and removes Saeb et al. (2015). Its central positioning around clinically grounded narratives from real sensor streams remains unchanged.

P1.justification: V2 makes targeted introductory additions, rewrites and condenses limitations and ethics passages, corrects wording and notation, and adds acknowledgments. The main section sequence and most method, results, and appendix prose remain intact.

P2.justification: V2 adds four analysis tables, relocates existing figures and tables, and renumbers the expert-background and prompt-template tables. Some captions and architecture labels change, while the existing plots, qualitative examples, and overall two-column design are retained.

improvement.justification: V2 strengthens evidence for sensor dependence through the new mismatch control and improves transparency about access, recruitment, and intended clinical use. These are useful, limited gains over the unchanged headline evaluations. They are partly offset by overstated robustness: Table 7 shows summary alignment changing from 0.545 to 0.574, exceeding the claimed 0.01 bound.
